title: The long wait
hook: survivors, many of them widows, waited decades for justice, while the years that followed brought violence to many Punjabi families of every background

segments.voice: Yesterday, yaad: thousands of Sikhs killed by mobs, and neighbors who hid neighbors. Your line was they had names. Today, the people who carried those names for decades after. Day three hundred eleven.

In west Delhi there's a neighborhood people have long called the Widow Colony. After November 1984, many women who had lost husbands, sons and brothers in a few days were moved there, into small flats, often with young children. They went to work. They raised their kids. And year after year, they went to hearings, stood in front of commissions, and told the same story again. Some of them grew old doing it. Some died before any court said a word. Today: the long wait.
screen: `THE WIDOW COLONY.` → `WORK, CHILDREN, HEARINGS.` → `YEAR AFTER YEAR.`

segments.voice: After November 1984, there were many inquiries. Commission after commission, committee after committee, around ten of them over twenty years. Reports were written. Few people were punished. In 2005, the Prime Minister, himself a Sikh, apologized in parliament. In 2018, more than thirty years later, a court sentenced a senior politician to life in prison for his part. For the widows, some of it came too late, and some has never come. And the long wait wasn't only in Delhi. In Punjab, the years after 1984 brought a decade of violence that reached families of every background. Armed militants killed many people: Hindus, Sikhs who opposed them, police, bus passengers. In 1985 a bomb on an Air India flight from Canada killed three hundred twenty-nine people; a Canadian inquiry blamed militants based in Canada, though only one man was ever convicted. And the state's response was harsh too: young Sikh men were detained, and many disappeared. A Sikh human rights worker named Jaswant Singh Khalra went through cremation records in Amritsar and found thousands of bodies burned as unidentified. In 1995 he was taken from outside his home and killed. Police officers were later convicted. So the wait belongs to many: widows in Delhi, mothers in Punjab still asking where a son went, families who lost someone to a militant's gun. Sikh teaching speaks of the Guru's justice, and of standing for the oppressed. And this is why the line matters: justice delayed still matters. A verdict after thirty years can't give anyone back. But it says out loud that a wrong was a wrong, and that the names count.
screen: `TEN INQUIRIES, FEW PUNISHED.` · `AN APOLOGY, A VERDICT, DECADES ON.` · `VIOLENCE FOR EVERY BACKGROUND.` · `KHALRA AND THE CREMATION RECORDS.` · then, large: `JUSTICE DELAYED STILL MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold those still waiting for justice. Settle, and breathe. Think of anyone, anywhere, who is still waiting: a family asking for answers, a person whose case is stuck, a community whose wrong was never named. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, simply keep them in mind, and wish them strength for the waiting. Notice if anger comes. Let it be there without feeding it. Then return to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Insaaf. Justice — the word on banners as survivors of 1984, many of them widows, waited decades for it, while violence reached Punjabi families of every background.
Your line: justice delayed still matters. Today, if someone tells you about a wrong done to them long ago, don't say move on. Say, that mattered. Day three hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Sikh organizations and families of 1984 survivors continue to press for justice through the courts, and each November gatherings remember the dead and the widows who waited.

original.note: Punjabi (from Persian): insaaf, justice; the word on many banners at 1984 remembrances.

what a scholar hears: about ten commissions and committees examined November 1984; Sajjan Kumar was sentenced to life by the Delhi High Court in December 2018.

notes: Balance: this day names militant violence (including Air India 182) alongside state violence (disappearances, the Khalra case), as the outline asks ('every background'). Keeper to review carefully for tone and to confirm nothing ranks one suffering over another.
Manmohan Singh's apology in the Rajya Sabha, August 2005; Sajjan Kumar's conviction, December 2018. Confirm.
Khalra's figures (thousands of cremations in Amritsar district) and the later conviction of police officers: confirm.

Air India 182: softened from 'planted by militants' as settled fact to the Canadian inquiry's finding (Major Commission, 2010) plus the single conviction (Inderjit Singh Reyat); Malik and Bagri were acquitted in 2005. Keeper to confirm wording.
